summary:
This A/B run covered 7 chat-based evals on an EKS compliance-overlay agent, each run 3 times per variant. Across most evals, with_skill met the expected output and assertion criteria more often than without_skill, often by a wide margin, but there are important nuances and caveats to weigh.

**Expected output / assertions pattern:**
- In 5 of 7 evals (eks-overlay-cis-542-public-endpoint, eks-overlay-delta-classification, eks-overlay-vuln-no-invented-cve, eks-overlay-fleet-drift, eks-overlay-not-requested), with_skill met expected output and passed assertions at a much higher rate than without_skill (e.g. with_skill 100% vs without_skill 0-33% on several). Many of these had assertions that with_skill always passed (3/3) while without_skill always failed (0/3), a clean "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" pattern — a real, consistent divergence, not noise.
- In eks-overlay-eks-overlay-compliance-derivation, both variants struggled: with_skill met expected output 1/3 and without_skill 0/3, with the underlying trigger itself only firing 1/3 of the time. All assertions here were "flaky" for with_skill and uniformly failing for without_skill — this looks more like a weak trigger/task setup than a strong signal favoring either variant.
- In eks-overlay-delta-identity-mismatch, the pattern reverses: without_skill met expected output 3/3 while with_skill only 1/3, and without_skill's assertion pass rate (78%) was decent though not perfect, while with_skill hit 100% on its (very small, 1-sample-per-iteration) assertion set. Confidence on without_skill's expected-output judgment here was "medium," and the trigger itself only fired 1/3 of the time for this eval, so this is a lower-confidence, partial result rather than a strong contrast.

**Assertions passing for both or neither:** Several individual assertions (e.g. "CIS 5.4.1 as PASS," "CIS 5.4.2 as FAIL," "does not compute New/Resolved/Regressed classes," "vpc-cni lag labeled as version gap") passed consistently for both variants — these aren't differentiating and indicate the behavior itself is solid for both. A few assertions in eks-overlay-fleet-drift are marked "inconclusive" for without_skill because no assertion data exists for that variant in that eval.

**Quality comparison:** Direct quality comparisons were largely unavailable — most evals had 0 pairs evaluated and quality comparisons skipped (2-3 pairs skipped per eval), so little can be said about output quality head-to-head. The one eval with a quality pair evaluated (eks-overlay-cis-542-public-endpoint) favored without_skill on one criterion (actionability) at medium confidence, with accuracy and completeness "comparable" — a thin, low-volume signal.

**Runtime and cost:** Mixed and generally small in absolute terms. Variant_b was faster/cheaper in some evals (e.g. eks-overlay-vuln-no-invented-cve: 11s/$0.10 vs without_skill's 30s/$0.25; eks-overlay-cis-542-public-endpoint: 15s vs 21s) and slower/costlier in others (eks-overlay-eks-overlay-compliance-derivation: 5s vs 4s; eks-overlay-fleet-drift: 31s vs 26s; eks-overlay-not-requested: 6s vs 3s). None of these differences are large enough on their own to be decisive, especially set against the much larger differences seen in expected-output pass rates.

**Consistency across repeated runs:** Where measured, with_skill was mostly "mostly_consistent" (scores ~2.3-2.7/3) across evals, with one eval (eks-overlay-delta-classification) scored "inconsistent" (1.33/3) — meaning with_skill's own outputs varied notably run-to-run there despite comparatively higher assertion pass rates. without_skill's consistency was null (not measured/not applicable) for most evals except two, where it scored "mostly_consistent" to "consistent." This asymmetry in data availability means consistency conclusions are patchy and shouldn't be over-interpreted for either variant.

**Overall picture:** with_skill met expected outputs and passed assertions more often than without_skill in the majority of evals, sometimes very clearly (clean pass/fail splits on several assertions), while one eval showed the reverse (without_skill ahead on expected output, with lower confidence) and one eval was weak/inconclusive for both variants due to a low trigger-fire rate. Quality-criterion comparisons and some consistency data are sparse (many skipped pairs, nulls for without_skill), limiting how much can be concluded about overall output quality or run-to-run stability beyond the pass-rate findings. Runtime/cost differences were present but modest and mixed in direction, not a decisive factor relative to the assertion-level differences.

eks-overlay-compliance-derivation.summary:
This single chat-task eval covered a CIS benchmark-mapping scenario run 3 times for each variant, with 5 assertions checked per run (15 assertion checks total per variant).

Trigger/behavior firing: The underlying behavior under test only fired in 1 of 3 runs overall (33%), so for 2 of the 3 runs there was effectively nothing to evaluate against the expected output - this limits how much weight any single run's pass/fail can carry.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 1 of 3 runs (33%), without_skill in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Confidence behind these judgments is high and not flagged as low-confidence, so the measurement itself is considered reliable, even though the sample size (3 runs) is small.

Assertions: Across all 5 assertions (checked 3 times each = 15 checks), with_skill passed 5/15 (33%) and without_skill passed 0/15 (0%). Notably, every one of the 5 individual assertions shows the identical pattern: with_skill passes 1/3 runs and without_skill passes 0/3 runs, each marked "flaky" for with_skill. This means no assertion distinguishes the variants with a clean pass/fail - instead the pattern is uniform across all assertions, reflecting one single run where with_skill happened to succeed and without_skill did not, rather than 5 independently differentiating checks. No assertion passed consistently for either variant, and none passed for without_skill at all, suggesting this task/assertion set is challenging or inconsistently triggered for both variants, with with_skill succeeding in only a fraction of attempts.

Quality comparison: No quality comparison pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this eval.

Runtime/cost: Very similar for both — with_skill averaged 5s/$0.05 vs without_skill's 4s/$0.04. These differences are small and likely not meaningful on their own, especially given the larger gaps seen in correctness.

Output consistency: Data here is asymmetric — with_skill has no consistency score reported (null), while without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, medium confidence) across its repeated runs. Since with_skill lacks a comparable score, no direct consistency comparison can be made.

Overall state: The clearest and most consistent signal is that with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions in 1 of 3 runs, while without_skill did not meet the expected output or pass any assertion in any of the 3 runs. However, the low trigger-fire rate (1/3 overall) and small sample size (3 runs) mean this is based on very limited data, and quality/consistency comparisons are largely missing (no quality pairs evaluated, no consistency score for with_skill). Runtime and cost differences between variants are minor and not decisive. Overall, this is a small, partial dataset showing a directional difference favoring with_skill on correctness, but with substantial gaps in the data (trigger firing, quality, and consistency comparisons) that limit how strong a conclusion can be drawn.

eks-overlay-cis-542-public-endpoint.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-based eval (3 repeated runs) testing whether the agent correctly handles CIS benchmark checks 5.4.1/5.4.2 alongside a prior evidence item (AX12).

Trigger behavior: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs for both variants (100%), so the scenario was properly exercised.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%, high confidence). without_skill met it in only 1 of 3 runs (33%, high confidence). This is a clear, high-confidence gap on the top-level success measure, not a borderline or low-confidence finding.

Assertions (per-run checks): with_skill passed all 12/12 assertion instances; without_skill passed 9/12 (75%). Breaking this down by individual assertion is informative: three of the four assertions passed consistently for both variants ("CIS 5.4.1 as PASS," "CIS 5.4.2 as FAIL due to endpointPublicAccess," and "deciding 5.4.2 from the already-recorded AX12 evidence") — these are not differentiating and show both variants handle the core compliance logic reliably. The remaining assertion ("AX12 remains PASS and is not regraded") passed 3/3 for with_skill but 0/3 for without_skill, both with high confidence — this single assertion accounts for the entire gap in both expected-output and assertion pass rates, indicating without_skill has a specific, repeatable issue with avoiding regrading of previously-passed evidence.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for quality (2 were skipped), so this dimension has limited coverage. In the one comparable pair, without_skill was favored overall and specifically on "actionability" (medium confidence); accuracy and completeness were rated comparable (tied) between the two. Given only one pair was assessed, this finding is suggestive rather than robust.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 15s and $0.13 per run; without_skill averaged 21s and $0.18 — with_skill was faster and cheaper by a moderate margin, though both stayed well under the 30s threshold with no runs exceeding it (only 1 pair evaluated for this metric).

Context usage: Both variants used minimal context (4.5–4.9% utilization) with no compaction events — no meaningful difference here.

Output consistency: Both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" across repeated runs. without_skill scored marginally higher on the consistency scale (2.67 vs 2.33, both high confidence), meaning without_skill's outputs varied slightly less run-to-run, though both were in the same qualitative consistency band.

Overall picture: The dominant, high-confidence finding is that without_skill failed to meet the expected output in 2 of 3 runs due to a specific, repeatable failure to treat AX12 as already-passed/non-regraded evidence, while with_skill handled this correctly every time. Other assertions show no difference between variants. Separately, with_skill was somewhat faster and cheaper, while without_skill showed a slight edge in output consistency and was favored in a single (low-coverage) quality comparison on actionability. These secondary dimensions are tradeoffs with limited evaluation depth, and should be weighed as such alongside the clearer expected-output/assertion gap.

eks-overlay-delta-classification.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested whether the agent correctly classified findings across a review (S1 Resolved, S2 Persisting, R6 Regressed, AX5 New; O12 Unverified), explained its matching methodology, and placed a delta summary in the right location. The triggering behavior itself fired in all 3 runs for both variants, so the scenario was exercised as intended.

On meeting the expected output, with_skill passed in 2 of 3 runs (67%, medium confidence) while without_skill passed in 0 of 3 runs (0%, high confidence) — a clear, consistent gap, and the high-confidence rating on without_skill's failures means this isn't a weak/noisy judgment.

At the per-assertion level, the same pattern holds throughout: with_skill passed 9/12 assertion-checks (75%) versus without_skill's 0/8 (0%). Every one of the four distinct assertions (classification correctness, O12 handling, fingerprint-matching explanation, and delta subsection placement) was failed in all without_skill runs, while with_skill passed the classification assertion in all 3 runs and passed the other three in 2 of 3 runs each (pattern labeled 'flaky' for those three). So with_skill's results are not perfectly stable either — it shows run-to-run variation on three of the four checks — but it still substantially outperformed without_skill on every assertion measured. No assertion passed for both variants or failed for both, so each one meaningfully differentiates the variants in this run.

Runtime and cost were close and not a differentiating factor: with_skill averaged 21s/$0.18 versus without_skill's 23s/$0.20, a small difference in both directions-adjacent dimensions. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~4-4.5%, no compaction).

The quality-comparison dimension could not be used: all 3 pairs were skipped, so there is no side-by-side quality judgment available here.

Output consistency was only computed for with_skill, which came back "inconsistent" overall (score 1.33/with 2 of 3 dimensions flagged inconsistent, 1 mostly consistent, high confidence in that judgment) — reinforcing the flakiness seen in its assertion results. No consistency data exists for without_skill in this report, so no comparison can be made there; this is an absence of data, not a sign that without_skill was more or less consistent.

Overall, the clearest, best-supported signal here is that without_skill failed to meet the expected output or satisfy any assertion in this eval, while with_skill succeeded on most assertions/checks but with some internal run-to-run inconsistency. Cost, runtime, and quality-comparison data do not add meaningful differentiation given skipped pairs and minor metric differences."

eks-overlay-delta-identity-mismatch.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task run 3 times each for without_skill and with_skill, examining whether the agent correctly handles a delta/report comparison scenario (New/Resolved/Regressed classes, identity-mismatch handling).

Trigger and expected output: The underlying "trigger" behavior being tested only fired in 1 of 3 runs overall (33%), which limits confidence in this measurement generally. On expected-output matching, without_skill passed in all 3 of its runs (100%), while with_skill passed in only 1 of 3 (33%). without_skill's expected-output confidence was rated "medium" (not low, but not the strongest), while with_skill's was rated "high" — meaning with_skill's lower pass rate is backed by a more confident judgment, and without_skill's higher pass rate carries slightly more uncertainty than the raw numbers suggest.

Assertions: Aggregate pass rates show with_skill at 3/3 (100%) and without_skill at 7/9 (78%), but with_skill was only evaluated on 1 run's worth of assertions (3 total, one per assertion) versus without_skill's 9 (3 runs × 3 assertions), so the comparison is based on much thinner data for with_skill. Looking per-assertion: one assertion ("does not compute New/Resolved/Regressed classes") passed consistently for both variants across all runs — this assertion isn't distinguishing the two. The other two assertions (about requiring a prior report for delta, and rendering delta overlay as unavailable with identity-mismatch reason rather than skipping silently) each passed 100% for with_skill's single run but were flaky for without_skill, passing 2 of 3 runs — meaning without_skill's behavior varied run-to-run on these points, while with_skill's single observed run passed cleanly. Given with_skill only has one run of assertion data, it's unclear whether with_skill would also show flakiness over more trials.

Metrics: with_skill had a measurable runtime (~4s average) and cost (~$0.04 average), while without_skill showed 0s runtime and $0.00 cost — the latter may indicate a caching/short-circuit path, measurement gap, or a fundamentally different execution flow rather than a true "faster/cheaper" comparison; this should be interpreted cautiously. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~4% and ~3.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison and consistency: No quality comparison pairs could be evaluated (all 3 were skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this task. Output consistency metrics are null for both variants, so run-to-run consistency cannot be assessed directly from that dimension, though the flaky assertion pattern for without_skill suggests some run-to-run variability in its behavior.

Overall, the data here is thin and partly asymmetric (with_skill's assertion and expected-output numbers rest on a single run tested against a low trigger-fire rate of 33%, while without_skill has more runs but shows flakiness on two of three assertions and a lower overall assertion pass rate). No quality or consistency comparisons are available, and the runtime/cost figures for without_skill look anomalous (zero) and warrant verification rather than being taken as a clear efficiency advantage.

eks-overlay-vuln-no-invented-cve.summary:
This single chat eval ran 3 trials. The trigger behavior fired consistently (3/3), so the underlying scenario was properly exercised for both variants.

On meeting the expected output, with_skill passed all 3 of its trials (3/3, 100%) with high-confidence judgments, while without_skill failed both of its evaluated trials (0/2, 0%, medium confidence — note only 2 of its runs were scored here, one fewer than with_skill). This is a fairly stark and consistent gap, though the medium confidence on without_skill's judgments means that result should be read as reasonably but not maximally certain.

Per-assertion results (12 checks for with_skill, 8 for without_skill) echo this pattern: both variants fully passed the assertion about labeling the vpc-cni lag as a version gap rather than a confirmed vulnerability (an assertion that both pass, so it doesn't differentiate them). Two other assertions — about noting that Inspector findings don't cover AWS-hosted add-on images, and about placing the summary in a "Vulnerability posture" subsection — were passed 100% by with_skill but failed 0% by without_skill, driving most of the overall gap. One assertion, about the overlay using already-collected evidence with no new reads, was flaky for with_skill (2/3, 67%) and failed entirely for without_skill (0/2), suggesting this particular check is inconsistently satisfied regardless of variant and may need attention on its own. Overall assertion pass rates were 11/12 (92%) for with_skill versus 2/8 (25%) for without_skill.

On runtime and cost, with_skill was notably faster (~11s vs ~30s) and cheaper (~$0.10 vs ~$0.25) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.7% vs 4.0%), with no compaction events for either.

Direct quality comparison between the two variants could not be assessed: all 3 pairs were skipped, leaving zero pairs evaluated, so there is no head-to-head quality verdict available from that dimension.

Output consistency was measured only for with_skill, which was "mostly consistent" across repeated runs (score 2.67/3, with 2 dimensions rated fully consistent and 1 mostly consistent, high confidence).
